Design: RAG over 10M internal documents

The index is 58 GB, not 209 — and permissions decide the architecture before the vector store does

Ten million documents will never fit in front of a model, so the system does not try. Offline it splits every document into passages of a few hundred words and files each passage twice: once by meaning, so that a question about “laptop replacement” finds a page titled “hardware refresh”, and once by exact words, so that a question about ticket INC-2024-00847 finds the one page containing that string. At question time it pulls about a hundred candidates from each store, ranks them with a slower and much more accurate model, keeps the best ten, and hands only those to the language model with an instruction to answer from them and cite where each claim came from.

Two stores, because meaning-search quietly averages away the exact token that discriminates — and an internal corpus is mostly ticket numbers, error codes and system names. A second ranking pass, because the first pass was tuned for speed over a very large pile. Citations, because the product is trust: an answer nobody can check is worth less than a search box.

The hard part is not the size. Thirty-four million passages fit in fifty-eight gigabytes of memory on one machine, and the search itself takes a few milliseconds. The hard part is that every employee is allowed to see a different corpus, so the permission check has to happen inside the search, before ranking. Do it afterwards and the people with the least access get a blank page and conclude the system is broken.

Like a librarian with a security clearance. She keeps two catalogues, one by subject and one by exact title, pulls a trolley from both, and skims it herself to put the best ten on top. What makes her job hard is not the size of the library: it is knowing which rooms you may enter before she takes anything off a shelf.

Size it before you draw. 10M documents at ~1,500 tokens is ~15B tokens; at 512-token chunks with 15% overlap that is ~34M chunks. At 1,536 dimensions in fp32 the raw vectors are 34M×1536×4B≈209 GB — a number that scares people into sharding. Then apply int8 scalar quantisation (4×, under 1% recall loss) for ~52 GB, add the HNSW graph at M=16 (N×M×2×4B≈4.4 GB) and ~1.4 GB of ID and version tracking: ~58 GB, one large-memory node, two for HA. The 209→58 step is the single most valuable thing you say in this prompt.

The request path, in order: gateway (authn, rate limit) → query understanding (rewrite, decompose, route) → semantic cache keyed on query plus tenant plus ACL hash → parallel fan-out to dense top-100 and BM25 top-100 with the ACL pre-filter applied inside both → fusion (tiered boosting, +7.5% NDCG, against +1.3% for plain RRF) → cross-encoder rerank 100→10 at 50–150 ms on GPU → context assembly under a token budget → input guardrail → streamed generation with citations → output guardrail, async and sampled. Offline: connectors and CDC queue → parse, preserving tables as markdown → recursive chunker at 512/50 → optional contextual enrichment → batched embedding → two sinks, vector and keyword → ACL sidecar keyed by chunk ID → index version registry. Emit chunk IDs, token counts and index version on every request or you cannot debug a single complaint.

Capacity is not the interesting constraint. 23 QPS against a store benchmarked at p50 4 ms / p99 25 ms per million vectors is comfortable inside one shard; the LLM is the bottleneck. Cost is: ~6,000 input and ~400 output tokens per query, 200K queries/day, is 1.2B input and 80M output tokens a day — $3,200/day, ~$96K/month at a mid-tier model and ~$12.6K/month at a Flash-class one. That 8× gap is larger than any infrastructure saving available anywhere else in this design, which is why routing is the first cost lever and sharding is not a cost lever at all.

Failure modes worth naming before you are asked. Right document, wrong section is a chunk-boundary artefact — fix with parent-document retrieval and contextual chunk headers, and measure section-level context recall rather than chunk-level. Embedding migration invalidates the index: you cannot mix vector spaces, so it is dual-index, shadow evaluate, ramp, roll back, with the re-embed budgeted as a recurring line item. Prompt injection via a wiki page: retrieved text is data, never instruction, delimited as such — and this system holds no tool authority at all, which is the cheapest defence on the table and worth saying. Stale semantic cache after an edit: invalidate by document ID on ingest, not by TTL alone. ACL drift: re-check permissions at query time against live groups, never the snapshot taken at ingestion. And the eval trap — recall@10 of 0.91 with faithfulness 0.6 is a system that confidently invents answers out of the correct documents.

Be honest about which numbers are which. The 34M chunks, the 209→58 GB sizing and the $96K/month are derived arithmetic from published unit prices, compression ratios and Qdrant’s graph formula — not benchmarks anyone ran on your corpus. The compression ratios themselves (4× at under 1% recall loss, 32× binary at 5–15%) and the vector-store latencies are measured. Present arithmetic as arithmetic; an interviewer who catches you passing off a calculation as a benchmark discounts every other number you gave.

Ask these before you draw anything

  • Do documents carry per-user permissions?Yes — and this is the constraint that shapes the whole design. Ask it in the first two minutes.
  • How many users, how many queries?~20,000 employees at ~10 queries a day: 200K/day, 2.3 QPS average, ~23 QPS peak.
  • Q&A with citations, or search with snippets?Q&A with citations users can click through. That makes grounding a product requirement, not a nicety.
  • What is the latency SLO?p95 under 2 s to first token, streaming. Which means you are budgeting TTFT, not total generation time.
  • How fresh must the index be?Minutes for high-traffic sources, hours for the tail. Tier it by source rather than promising real time.
  • What is the document mix and average length?Wikis, Docs, PDFs, Slack, Jira. Mixed formats, ~3 pages, call it 1,500 tokens.
  • What does “good” mean, and who judges it?Grounded answers with correct citations, against a golden set curated by internal comms and support.
  • Managed vector store or self-hosted?Managed unless data residency forbids it. At this scale it is not a scale decision.

The numbers you design against

  • CORPUS15B tokens10M documents at ~1,500 tokens each
  • CHUNKS34M512 tokens, 15% overlap
  • PEAK LOAD23 QPS2.3 average, 10× peak factor
  • INDEX IN RAM58 GBint8 plus graph, down from 209 GB
  • TTFT SLO2 s p95streamed, so first token is what is measured
  • SERVING BILL~$96K/month~$12.6K on a Flash-class model — same design

The interviewer is really testing

  • Whether you ask about per-user permissions before you draw a single box
  • Whether you can size the index in your head and land on one node, not a cluster
  • Whether “we would evaluate it” is a sentence or an actual system with gates
  • Whether you know what upgrading the embedding model costs, and how you cut over

The trap

Saying “we fetch the best ten and then drop the ones the user is not allowed to see”. That filter runs too late, and it does not fail loudly: it fails as an empty page for exactly the people with the narrowest access, who then report that the system is broken. The other one is answering “we would just re-embed everything” when asked about upgrading the meaning-search model. You cannot mix two of those models in one index, so the real answer is a second index built alongside, compared on a fixed test set, ramped, and reversible — with the re-embedding bill named out loud.

Saying “we retrieve the top ten and then filter out what the user cannot see”. That is post-filtering, and it fails silently as an empty result set for precisely the users with the narrowest access — who read it as a broken product, not as a permission boundary. Pre-filter inside both retrievers instead and pay the recall-tuning cost. The second version of the trap: “we would just re-embed everything” when asked about an embedding upgrade. You cannot mix vector spaces, so the answer is a dual index, a shadow eval, a ramp and a rollback, priced — ~$345 at text-embedding-3-small, ~$2,240 at large, plus ~$15,300 if you are keeping contextual enrichment.

The arithmetic, out loud derived, not benchmarked

corpus10M docs x 1,500 tokens15B tokens
chunks15B x 1.15 / 51234M chunks
raw vectors, fp3234M x 1,536 x 4 B209 GB
int8, 4x, <1% recall loss209 / 452 GB
HNSW graph, M = 1634M x 16 x 2 x 4 B4.4 GB
ids and versions34M x 40 B1.4 GB
RAM per replicaone node, two for HA58 GB

Every row above is arithmetic you perform in the room, not a benchmark: the inputs are published unit sizes and compression ratios, the results are yours. The one to say slowly is 209 to 58 — it converts “we will need a cluster” into “we will need a machine, and a second one for failover”.

The math one replica, HNSW

RAM=vectorsN×D×b​​+HNSW graphN×M×2×4B​​+ids and versionsN×40B​​What it does not say: b is a decision, not a constant. int8 is 4× at under 1% recall loss, binary is 32× at 5–15%. Choose the compression against your recall target first, then read the RAM number off this line.

The tradeoffs, and the sentence you say

  • DENSE VS HYBRIDHybrid, and not as a hedge. Argue it with the concrete failure: “a query for INC-2024-00847 will not be answered by cosine similarity.” The fusion step is worth arguing too — plain RRF buys +1.3% NDCG over BM25, tiered boosting +7.5%.
  • RERANK VS LATENCYTake the reranker, then make it the first rung you drop. A cross-encoder costs 50–150 ms on GPU and one report puts P@10 at 0.62 → 0.84. Under load, degrade to fusion-only and keep answering rather than shedding requests.
  • CHUNK SIZE512 with overlap, plus parent-document retrieval. Small chunks retrieve better and answer worse: semantic chunking hit 91.9% retrieval recall and still lost end to end, 54% against 69% for recursive 512. Fix the answer with a bigger parent, not a smaller chunk.
  • PERMISSIONS IN OR AFTERPre-filter, inside both retrievers. Post-filtering is one line of code and it produces empty result sets for restricted users, which reads as “this is broken” rather than “this is not for you”. Pre-filtering costs recall tuning effort; that is the whole price.
  • FRESHNESS VS COSTTier by source. Minutes for policy docs and runbooks, nightly for the archive. Real-time indexing of every Slack message is expensive and nobody has ever asked for it.
  • MANAGED VS SELF-HOSTEDNot a scale decision at all. At 34M vectors and 23 QPS both work. It is a data-residency and operational-headcount decision — say that instead of benchmarking, because reaching for a benchmark here is the wrong instinct on display.

Where the retrieval numbers come from

Anthropic’s contextual retrieval work (September 2024) prepends a short generated context header to each chunk before embedding. Top-20 retrieval failure fell from 5.7% to 3.7%; adding contextual BM25 took it to 2.9%, a 49% reduction; adding reranking took it to 1.9%, a 67% reduction. The header generation costs $1.02 per million document tokens, which on this 15B-token corpus is ~$15,300 one-off — a real line item, and the part people leave out when they quote the 67%.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

A user asks a question whose answer is spread across four documents. What breaks?
The shortlist fills up with four copies of the same thing. Each passage is scored on its own, so the ten that look most like the question are usually ten versions of the same paragraph rather than one from each document. The model answers confidently from a quarter of the evidence, and every citation it gives you checks out, which is what makes it hard to spot. Fix it by forcing the shortlist to be varied rather than merely similar, by splitting the question into parts and searching each part, and by tagging these cases in your test set so you can see the problem come back.
Top-k breaks, and it breaks quietly. Ranking scores each chunk independently, so the shortlist fills with four near-duplicates of the single best-matching passage instead of one passage from each source — and the model then answers confidently from a quarter of the evidence, with citations that all look correct. Three fixes in cost order: diversity-aware selection (MMR) at the fusion step so near-identical chunks stop crowding each other out; query decomposition into sub-questions with a union of results; and a multi-hop tag in the golden set so the regression is visible next time. Skip the third and you will not notice when it returns.
Cut serving cost by 5x without a quality drop users notice. Go.
Send the easy questions to the cheap model. Roughly seven in ten queries are simple lookups a small model answers just as well, and that single decision is most of the difference between about ninety-six thousand dollars a month and about thirteen thousand. Then stop paying full price to re-read the same instructions on every request — cached reading costs about a tenth. Then send five passages instead of ten, but only once you have checked the answer still sits inside the five. Order matters: routing first, because the other two are rounding errors beside it.
Routing does most of it, and you should say so before you list anything else. A small classifier sends the ~70% of queries that are simple lookups to a Flash-class model and keeps the frontier model for synthesis — that alone is most of the distance between ~$96K and ~$12.6K a month. Then prefix caching on the system prompt, where cached reads bill at ~10% of the input rate. Then shrink context from 10 chunks to 5, but only after checking that context precision supports it. Together these plausibly reach 5×; that total is derived arithmetic rather than a measured result, so quote it as an estimate and name what would move it.
How do you know it got better?
Two scores, never one. Measure separately whether the right passages were found, and whether the answer actually followed from them. A system can be excellent at the first and poor at the second, which is the worst failure you can ship: correct sources, invented answer, and it looks convincing. Build a few hundred real failed questions into a fixed test set, check that your automatic grader agrees with human graders before you trust it, block a release that drops more than five percent on either score, and keep grading a tenth of live traffic afterwards.
Two layers of metric, measured separately, or you are shipping blind. Build a golden set of 300–1,000 cases harvested from real failures and tagged by failure mode. Calibrate the judge against 100 human labels until Spearman is ≥0.85 — 0.70 is only good enough for low-stakes work. Gate CI at faithfulness 0.85 and context recall 0.80 with a 5% regression tolerance, then sample 10% of live traffic and alert when rolling faithfulness falls below 0.75. The reason to keep the layers apart: recall@10 of 0.91 alongside faithfulness of 0.6 is a system confidently inventing answers from the correct documents, and any single blended score hides exactly that case.

No-hire answer vs strong answer

No hire

Draws documents → embeddings → vector database → LLM, names a vector database brand as though that were the design, never computes the index size, never mentions permissions, treats “we would evaluate it” as a sentence rather than a system, and answers the embedding-upgrade question with “we would re-embed everything” — no cost, no cutover, no dual index.

Strong

Asks about permissions in the first two minutes and calls it the hardest part. Computes 34M chunks and 209 GB → 58 GB out loud. Picks hybrid retrieval and justifies it with a ticket ID rather than with “best of both worlds”. Names the right-document-wrong-section failure before being asked. Prices the re-index. Separates retrieval metrics from generation metrics and attaches a number to each.

Say this back tomorrow

Thirty-four million passages, each a list of 1,536 numbers. At four bytes a number that is 209 gigabytes; at one byte a number, plus the search graph, it is 58. One machine, two for safety.
34M×1536×4B=209 GB  ·  int8 + graph  ·  58 GB
  • Permissions decide the architecture; the vector store brand is a detail
  • Size the index twice — raw and quantised — and say both numbers
  • At this scale the LLM is the bottleneck, so cost work means routing, not sharding

Unlocks

  • hybrid retrieval
  • cross-encoder rerank
  • ACL pre-filter
  • semantic cache
  • golden set and judge

Design: an inference layer for a 70B model

KV cache memory is the binding constraint, and quantisation is a ten-fold cost decision rather than a speed tweak

A 70-billion-parameter model does not fit on one graphics card, so the first decision is how many cards hold one copy and how much room is left over. Two cards give you 160 gigabytes. The model’s weights take 140 of that at full precision, and about ten more disappear into framework overhead, which leaves roughly ten gigabytes for the part nobody expects to matter: the scratch memory each conversation keeps alive while it is being answered.

That scratch memory is the whole design. Every token in a request — prompt and reply — leaves behind about a third of a megabyte that has to stay resident until the request finishes. At fifteen hundred tokens a request, ten gigabytes of headroom holds about twenty conversations at once. Store the weights and the scratch at half the precision and the same two cards hold about three hundred and twenty-five. Serving ten thousand people at once is then either six hundred and sixty-six cards or sixty-two, which is roughly one and a half million dollars a month against a hundred and thirty thousand. Same model, same service level, one decision.

Everything else in the design protects that pool of scratch memory. Requests queue in front of a scheduler that keeps a batch running and slots new work in as old work finishes, instead of waiting for a whole batch to end. Traffic that shares the same long instructions is sent to the same machine so the work of reading them is done once. A small pool of machines is kept warm and idle, because starting one takes about a minute and most traffic spikes are shorter than that — and the idle time is paid for by letting overnight batch jobs run there.

Like a restaurant kitchen with a very small pass. The chefs and the recipes are fixed cost; what actually limits how many tables you serve is the counter space where half-finished plates wait. Every diner occupies a slice of that counter from first course to last. Buying more chefs does nothing once the counter is full, and using smaller plates doubles the covers.

Start at memory, because memory is the constraint and everything else is downstream of it. Weights: 70B×2B=140 GB at BF16, 70 GB at FP8, 35 GB at INT4, plus 15–20% for activations, framework and CUDA context. KV cache per token for this architecture (80 layers, 8 KV heads via GQA, head dim 128) is 2×80×8×128×2B=0.327 MB, halving to 0.164 MB at FP8. On a 2×H100 shard: BF16 leaves 160−140−10≈10 GB for KV, and a 1,500-token request needs 0.49 GB, so ~20 concurrent. FP8 leaves ~80 GB against 0.25 GB per request, so ~325 concurrent. For 10,000 in flight that is ~62 H100s, against the ~666 the published BF16 walkthrough lands on, and at Lambda’s $2.99/GPU-hr that is ~$1.43M/month against ~$133K/month. Quantisation here is a ten-fold cost decision, not a speed tweak.

Now the sizing trap, and say it before they spring it. If those users make 1M requests a day at 500 output tokens, that is 500M output tokens/day, about 5,800 tokens/s on average, and one H100 running this model at FP8 and concurrency 100 produces 2,400–2,780 tokens/s — so average throughput needs about 3 GPUs. Concurrency sizing said 62. Both sums are correct; they answer different questions, and the gap is queueing and burstiness. “I am sizing on concurrency, because the SLO is TTFT” is the sentence that marks the level.

The path, in order: client → API gateway (auth, per-tenant rate limits, validation, SSE for streaming) → model router doing prefix-aware consistent hashing, so requests sharing a system prompt land on the same scheduler and hit its prefix cache → per-model scheduler owning the active batch and the waiting queue, doing continuous batching and admission control → workers owning GPUs, weights and a paged KV pool in 16-token blocks → optionally separate prefill and decode pools with a KV transfer path between them. Off the hot path: a warm standby pool, a batch queue that backfills idle capacity, and a metering pipeline emitting tokens and cost per tenant.

Failure modes. OOM under a long-context burst: preempt the longest-running request, swapping its KV to host memory or recomputing it, and let admission control refuse before the pool is exhausted rather than after. Client disconnects mid-stream: without cancellation propagation a client that opens and immediately closes connections DDoSes you while workers keep generating for nobody. Tenant runaway: one team’s retry loop eats the fleet, so per-tenant token-rate limits and a circuit breaker at 3× rolling spend. Cold start: ~62 s for vLLM and ~28 minutes if a TensorRT engine has to compile, so pre-compile engines in CI and ship artefacts — never compile in the serving path. Prefix cache thrash: prefix-blind routing turns one shared 2,000-token system prompt into a per-replica cost. Silent regression from a quantisation rollout: FP8 is a model change and goes through the model-change gates, not the config-change ones.

Which numbers are which matters. The weight sizes, the 0.327 MB/token, the throughput table and the 62-second cold start are published figures. The ~325 concurrent, the ~62 GPUs and the ~$133K/month are my arithmetic on top of them, and they assume every request holds 1,500 tokens of KV for its whole life — which overstates memory for short requests and understates it for long ones. The published walkthrough gets ~30 per BF16 shard where this gets ~20, on a different overhead assumption; the order is what is scored. Quote the band, not the digit.

Ask these before you draw anything

  • Can we quantise, if quality holds on the eval set?Yes — and it is the highest-leverage question in the prompt. It is the difference between ~666 GPUs and ~62.
  • How many models, and what sizes?One 70B, plus a small model for routing and classification. That second one pays for itself twice.
  • Interactive chat, or batch?Both. Which is what lets batch work backfill the idle capacity you are already paying for.
  • What are the SLOs?p95 TTFT under 500 ms interactive, inter-token under 50 ms. TTFT is the one that shapes the scheduler.
  • Peak concurrency?~10,000 in flight. Ask for concurrency, not QPS — concurrency is what holds memory.
  • Typical prompt and output length?~1,000 in, ~500 out. Call it 1,500 tokens of KV per request and carry that through every sum.
  • Multi-tenant: hard isolation, or accounting?Accounting and fair-share. That rules out per-tenant fleets before anyone proposes one.
  • What hardware is available?H100 80 GB, tensor-parallel across 2 GPUs. So the unit you are sizing is a 160 GB shard.

The numbers you design against

  • WEIGHTS140 / 70 / 35 GBBF16, FP8, INT4 — plus 15–20% overhead
  • KV PER TOKEN0.327 MB80 layers, 8 KV heads, head dim 128; 0.164 at FP8
  • PER 2×H100 SHARD~20 vs ~325concurrent 1,500-token requests, BF16 vs FP8
  • FLEET FOR 10K~666 vs ~62 GPUssame SLO, one quantisation decision apart
  • THE BILL$1.43M vs $133Kper month at Lambda’s $2.99/GPU-hr
  • COLD START62 svLLM; ~28 min if a TensorRT engine must compile

The interviewer is really testing

  • Whether you name the binding constraint before you name a serving framework
  • Whether you size on peak concurrency or on average throughput — and whether you notice which
  • Whether quantisation is a first-class decision or a footnote you add when pushed
  • Whether you have thought about the first sixty seconds after a deploy

The trap

Two sentences sink this round. The first is “we would put the standard serving framework behind a load balancer and scale up when the cards get busy” — scaling up takes about a minute to load the model, and most spikes are over before the new machine is ready. The second is quieter and worse: working out that the whole company only needs a few thousand tokens a second, dividing by what one card produces, and concluding you need about three cards. That sum is correct and the answer is twenty times too small, because it sizes for the average rather than for how many conversations are open at once — and it is open conversations that consume the memory.

Two sentences sink this round. The first: “we would run vLLM behind a load balancer and autoscale on GPU utilisation.” Reactive autoscaling cannot help when the cold start is ~62 s and the spike is shorter than the scale-up. The second is quieter and much worse: “500M output tokens a day over 2,400 tokens/s is about three H100s.” The arithmetic is correct and the answer is twenty-fold wrong, because it sizes for average throughput while the SLO is p95 TTFT and the memory is held by concurrent sequences, not by tokens per second. Name which of the two you are sizing on, out loud, and the trap disappears.

The arithmetic, out loud FP8 column; derived from sourced sizes

KV per request, FP81,500 tokens x 0.164 MB0.25 GB
free for KV on a 160 GB shard160 - 70 - 10 overhead~80 GB
concurrency per shard80 / 0.25~325 requests
fleet for 10,000 in flight10,000 / 325, x 2 GPUs~62 H100s

Run the same table at BF16 and you get ~10 GB free and ~20 per shard, so ~500 shards; the published walkthrough assumes ~30 per shard and lands on ~333 shards, or ~666 H100s. Either way it is an order of magnitude more hardware than FP8, which is the point. Both fleet numbers are derived arithmetic on top of sourced memory figures rather than measured throughput, and both assume every request holds its full 1,500 tokens for its whole life — say that out loud, because it is the first thing a good interviewer pokes.

The math per token, per request

KV bytes=2×L×Hkv​×dh​×seq×batch×bThe 2 is keys and values. Hkv​ is 8 rather than 64 because of grouped-query attention, and that factor of eight is the only reason serving a 70B model is affordable at all. What the formula hides: seq is the whole sequence, so a long-context request holds its memory for the entire generation.

The tradeoffs, and the sentence you say

  • CONTINUOUS VS STATIC BATCHINGContinuous, and be able to say why in one sentence. Static batching head-of-line blocks: a 50-token request and a 2,000-token request in the same batch both wait for the long one. Continuous batching over a paged KV pool gives 3–5× the effective batch size.
  • THROUGHPUT VS LATENCYSit deliberately near the knee, and know where it is. An H100 needs ~300 concurrent sequences before decode becomes compute-bound. Past that, aggregate throughput keeps rising while per-user latency degrades. Exactly where you sit is an SLO decision, not a framework default.
  • QUANTISATION VS QUALITYFP8, gated on the eval set. It roughly doubles achievable concurrency and cuts cost about ten-fold at fixed SLO here. Not free: A100s have no FP8 hardware acceleration, so on that generation you get the memory saving without the throughput saving.
  • DISAGGREGATE PREFILL AND DECODENot for a dense 70B at moderate batch. The wins are real elsewhere — 7× on GB200 NVL72 with Dynamo, and +61% req/s with a 50% TTFT cut at Baseten on ~50K-token prompts — but here the KV transfer can cost more than it saves. Say what would flip it: long contexts, MoE, higher concurrency.
  • REACTIVE VS PREDICTIVE SCALINGPredictive, plus warm standby. A ~62 s cold start is longer than most spikes, so reactive scaling always arrives after the incident. Pay for the standby by backfilling batch work onto it rather than by arguing for headroom.
  • FAIRNESS VS UTILISATIONFair-share with per-tenant token rates. Strict reservations strand GPUs; pure first-come-first-served lets one team’s batch job starve everyone else’s chat. Separate priority class for interactive traffic, and metering that makes the bill visible per team.

Where the latency actually goes

On a single H100 running Llama-3.3-70B at FP8, vLLM 0.18 goes from 120 tokens/s at concurrency 1 to 2,400 tokens/s at concurrency 100 — twenty times the throughput on the same card. Over that same range p95 TTFT goes from 68 ms to 1,450 ms. Nothing got slower; the queue got longer, and almost all of that 1,450 ms is waiting rather than computing. Baseten’s disaggregated prefill/decode rollout attacks exactly that layer and reports +61% requests/s with a 50% TTFT reduction on ~50K-token prompts.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Cut p95 time-to-first-token in half.
Look at the waiting, not the typing. Time to first token is mostly how long the request sat in a queue plus how long it took to read the prompt, not how fast the model writes. The same card answers in about seventy milliseconds with one user and takes almost a second and a half with a hundred — nothing about the hardware changed, the line got longer. So break long prompts into pieces that cannot block everyone behind them, reuse the work already done on the shared instructions, and cap how many requests you let in so the queue stays short. Buying more machines also works, and it is the most expensive way to shorten a queue.
Attack prefill and queueing — decode is not where the time is. TTFT is how long the request waited plus how long its prompt took to prefill, and the benchmark shows it: the same card goes from 68 ms p95 at concurrency 1 to 1,450 ms at concurrency 100. So: chunked prefill, so one long prompt cannot block the batch; prefix caching for the shared system prompt, which is free if the router is prefix-aware; and admission control to bound queue depth, trading a little throughput for the tail you are measured on. If long contexts dominate, disaggregate prefill and decode for the 50% TTFT cut Baseten reported. Adding GPUs works only through queue depth, and it is the most expensive way to buy it.
A team wants a fine-tuned variant. Do they get their own fleet?
No. Give them a small add-on layer that rides on the shared model. A separate copy needs its own seventy gigabytes and its own share of the machines, so every team that asks multiplies the bill. The add-on layers are a few hundred megabytes and can be swapped in per request against one shared copy. A team earns its own machines when its own traffic would keep those machines busy — that is a sum you can do with them in the room, not a policy you have to defend.
No — LoRA adapters on a shared base, swapped per request. A full fine-tune brings its own 70 GB of weights and its own KV pool, so every team that asks multiplies the fleet; adapters are a few hundred megabytes and ride the base model’s batch. Promote a variant to a dedicated fleet only when its own traffic would keep a shard busy, which is a utilisation sum you can do in front of them rather than a policy argument. The exception worth naming: if their variant changes the architecture or the quantisation, it is a different model and the adapter route is closed.
Speculative decoding: yes or no?
Yes when the machine is half idle, no when it is busy. The trick has a small fast model guess the next few words and the big model check them all in one pass. When only a handful of conversations are running, the big model spends most of its time waiting on memory, so the checking is nearly free and everyone gets answers sooner. When hundreds are running, the machine is already flat out on work that people are paying for, and the guesses compete with them. So switch it on for the interactive pool and off for the bulk one.
Yes at low concurrency, no at high, and the sign flips at the roofline. With few sequences in flight the GPU is memory-bound — it is streaming weights from HBM every step and the FLOPs are sitting idle — so a draft model verifying several tokens per pass buys real latency for free. Past the batching knee, around 300 concurrent sequences on an H100, decode is compute-bound and the draft competes for the same FLOPs as traffic that is already paying. So it is a per-pool decision: on for the interactive pool, off for the batch pool. “It is a knob whose sign depends on where you sit on the roofline” answers the question they actually asked.

No-hire answer vs strong answer

No hire

“We would use vLLM behind a load balancer with autoscaling.” Never computes weights or KV cache, sizes the fleet from average throughput without noticing which question that answers, and treats quantisation as a footnote to add if there is time at the end.

Strong

Identifies KV cache memory as the binding constraint inside three minutes. Computes 140 GB, 0.327 MB per token, ~20 against ~325 concurrent per shard, and produces both the ~666-GPU and the ~62-GPU fleet with the reason they differ. Notes that reactive autoscaling cannot beat a 62-second cold start. Catches the throughput-versus-concurrency sizing trap out loud. The published ladder is explicit here: SDE II names vLLM, SDE III names the KV cache constraint and scopes quantisation and speculative decoding unprompted, Principal frames the design as a portfolio of tradeoffs and asks when it breaks.

Say this back tomorrow

Every token in flight keeps about a third of a megabyte of scratch memory alive until its request finishes, or half that at reduced precision. Multiply by tokens per request, then by open requests. That product, not the model weights, is what runs out.
2×80×8×128×2B=0.327 MB/token  ·  ×1500×Nconcurrent​
  • Weights are the fixed cost; the KV cache is the variable one, and it is what runs out
  • Size on concurrency when the SLO is time to first token — size on throughput and you land twenty-fold low
  • A 62-second cold start rules out reactive autoscaling, so warm standby is not optional

Unlocks

  • paged KV cache
  • continuous batching
  • FP8 quantisation
  • prefix-aware routing
  • speculative decoding

Design: a customer-support agent

Pin down what “resolved” means before you draw anything, then put authority in the tool layer rather than the prompt

A message arrives on chat or email. A fast classifier checks it for abuse and for attempts to hijack the agent. A small, cheap model then decides which of four things it is: a question the help centre already answers, an account action, something genuinely complicated, or something out of scope. Roughly seven in ten are the first kind and never need the expensive model at all. For the rest a loop runs — the model proposes a step, a tool carries it out, the model reads the result — and it stops when the job is done or when it hits a hard limit: fifteen steps, a spending cap for that one conversation, and a check that it has not just called the same tool with the same arguments twice.

The structural decision is that the model never performs an action. It asks the tool layer, and a separate piece of ordinary software decides whether the action is allowed: who the customer is, whether the order qualifies, whether the refund sits under the value limit that needs a person to approve it. That software never reads the conversation, so nothing a customer types can argue it round. An invented refund is impossible in the same way an invalid amount is impossible — it never reaches the payment system.

The number everyone quotes is the one to distrust. There is no industry definition of “resolved”: handing a customer a set of instructions counts for some vendors, and a chat the customer abandoned in frustration counts for others. Insist on a written definition — closed without a human touch and not reopened within seven days — before you design, and measure how many customers come back beside it. Optimise the headline figure alone and you will build an agent that refuses to escalate.

Like a new call-centre agent with a locked till. They can look anything up, say anything reassuring, and start a refund — but the till only opens for amounts under the limit printed on their badge, and a supervisor holds the key for the rest. Training them better changes what they say. It never changes what the till does.

Pin the metric before the architecture, because everything downstream is scored against it. Intercom reports Fin averaging a 76% resolution rate under its own definition, which counts procedure handoffs; one FCA-regulated customer reports 60% inbound and 90% outbound under a definition it wrote itself. There is no standard — deflection is routinely counted as resolution, and so are abandoned chats. So write it down: closed with no human touch and no reopen within 7 days. Naming this problem unprompted is one of the strongest signals available in this prompt.

Sizing. 1M conversations/month is ~33K/day, 0.4/s average and ~1.2/s on promo days: not a throughput problem. Per conversation, 5 turns of (1,500 system + ~1,000 history + 2,000 retrieved + 800 tool schemas) is ~26,000 input tokens and ~1,500 output: $0.067 at a mid-tier model, ~$0.045 once you prefix-cache the ~2,300 static tokens per turn at ~10% of the input rate, ~$0.007 on a small model. So $45K/month against $7K, and the routing decision is the entire cost model. Latency: 5 turns at ~400 ms TTFT plus 150 output tokens at 20 ms, plus ~300 ms per tool call, is ~18 s p50 and 35–45 s p95 end to end — which is why the UI narrates “checking your order…” rather than showing a spinner.

The path, in order: channel adapters → conversation service (session state, history compaction) → input guardrail at <90 ms → intent router on a small model (FAQ / account action / complex / out of scope) → agent loop {plan, select tool, execute, observe} bounded by ~15 steps, a per-task dollar cap and repetition detection → tool layer behind a deterministic policy engine, where every tool carries an ACL, an idempotency key and a value threshold above which a human approves → hybrid retrieval with reranking over ~5,000 articles → generation with citations → output guardrail. Off the path: an escalation queue carrying the transcript, the tool trace and the agent’s stated hypothesis, and an eval pipeline sampling 10% of conversations plus 100% of escalations. History lives in a session store, long-term customer memory in the CRM read as a tool rather than stuffed into context, and the scratchpad outside the context window so long tasks do not degrade.

Failure modes. A loop that never terminates costs a published $50–500 before anyone notices: hard step cap, repetition detection at two identical calls, token budget, circuit breaker at 3× rolling hourly spend. Cost blowup from retries — one code-review agent charged $12 against a $0.40 average — so the dollar cap is per task, not only per tenant. Hallucinated action, an HR agent sending welcome emails on imagined acceptance status: verify against the source of truth before executing, and schema-validate every tool result. Prompt injection via the ticket or a retrieved review: untrusted-data framing, authority at the tool layer. Wrong-but-confident refund: idempotency keys, an approval threshold, daily reconciliation of AI-initiated financial actions. Escalation black hole: the handoff payload is a designed artefact, not a link to a transcript.

Which numbers are which. The resolution benchmarks, the guardrail thresholds and the incident costs are published. The $0.045 per conversation and the $45K-to-$7K span are derived from listed per-token prices and an assumed turn structure, and the 26,000 input tokens is the assumption to argue with, because moving it moves everything else. The $5–8 fully loaded cost of a human ticket is a standard planning estimate rather than a published figure — use it to make the point that cost is not the binding constraint here, not as evidence for anything finer.

Ask these before you draw anything

  • What does “resolve” mean, precisely?Closed with no human touch and no reopen within 7 days. Insist on it in writing — there is no industry standard.
  • What can the agent do, as opposed to say?Order lookup, address change, refunds under a threshold, subscription cancel. Everything else read-only.
  • Where is the human in the loop?Refunds above the threshold and anything flagged. The threshold is a business decision — ask for the number.
  • What volume, and how peaky?~1M conversations a month, 3× on promo days. Comfortably not a throughput problem.
  • Channel and latency expectation?Chat, streaming. First token under 2 s; users tolerate multi-second tool steps if the UI narrates them.
  • What is the knowledge base?~5,000 help-centre articles plus policy docs. Small enough that retrieval is solved if you rerank.
  • Regulated?Payments and returns policy, so an audit trail is required — which makes the tool trace a product requirement.
  • What is the cost ceiling?Under $0.10 per conversation. Comfortable, which tells you cost is not the binding constraint here.

The numbers you design against

  • VOLUME1M/month~33K/day, 0.4/s average, ~1.2/s on promo days
  • PER CONVERSATION~26K in, 1.5K out5 turns of system, history, context, schemas
  • COST~$0.045mid-tier with prefix caching; ~$0.007 on a small model
  • MONTHLY$45K vs $7Kthe routing decision, and essentially nothing else
  • END TO END~18 s p5035–45 s p95, so the UI narrates the tool steps
  • LOOP BOUNDS15 stepsrepetition at 2 identical calls, breaker at 3× spend

The interviewer is really testing

  • Whether you pin down what “resolved” means before designing against it
  • Whether authority lives in the tool layer or in a paragraph of prompt
  • Whether the loop has hard bounds with actual numbers on them
  • Whether you price a conversation without being asked to

The trap

Saying “we would prompt it carefully so it never promises a refund it cannot give”. An instruction is a request, not a control: the same message box that carries your instruction carries the customer trying to undo it. The safeguard has to be structural — the model asks, and separate software that never reads the chat decides. The second trap is quoting a resolution rate as though it meant the same thing everywhere. Ask what the number counts before you agree to be measured on it.

Saying “we would prompt it carefully so it does not promise a refund it cannot give”. A prompt is a request, not a control: the same channel that carries your instruction carries the customer writing “ignore your previous instructions” into the chat box. The control has to be structural — the model proposes, the policy engine disposes, and that engine never reads the conversation. The second version of the trap is quoting a resolution rate as if it were a standard measure: Fin’s 76% counts procedure handoffs, other vendors count abandoned chats, and nobody publishes a definition unless asked. Ask what the number counts.

The arithmetic, out loud derived from listed token prices

tokens per turn1,500 system + 1,000 history + 2,000 context + 800 schemas~5,300
per conversation5 turns x 5,300~26K in, 1.5K out
mid-tier model26K x $2/M + 1.5K x $10/M$0.067
with prefix caching2,300 static tokens at ~10% of input rate$0.045
small model instead$0.20 / $1.25 per M$0.007
1M conversations a monthroute ~70% to the small model$45K → $7K

A human ticket costs on the order of $5–8 fully loaded — a planning estimate, not a published figure. Against $0.045 the break-even deflection rate is so small that cost is not the binding constraint in this design. The cost of a wrong resolution is. Say that sentence out loud; it reframes the entire round, and it is the reason the policy engine gets the deep dive rather than the model choice.

The math per conversation

cost=input tokensT×(s+h+c+f)​​×pin​+out×pout​The term to attack is s+f — system prompt plus tool schemas — because it is static, repeated on every one of the T turns, and therefore cacheable at ~10% of the input rate. Shrinking c costs groundedness and shrinking h costs coherence, so cache the static part before you cut either.

The tradeoffs, and the sentence you say

  • AGENT LOOP VS WORKFLOWScripted workflow for the top 20 intents, agent loop for the tail. With an LLM only at the natural-language boundaries the common path is more reliable, cheaper and auditable. Over-engineering multi-agent systems where a workflow would do is on every published list of candidate pitfalls, and this is exactly where it happens.
  • AUTONOMY VS APPROVALThreshold-based approval, and ask for the threshold. Every irreversible action — refund, cancellation, address change on a shipped order — is a place where a hallucinated action becomes a real loss. The number is a business decision, and asking for it is part of the answer rather than a delay to it.
  • MODEL ROUTINGRoute ~70% of traffic to a small model. That one decision is the whole gap between $45K and $7K a month. Every other cost lever in this design is a rounding error beside it, so raise it before anyone asks about cost.
  • CONTEXT VS QUALITYCompact hard, keep durable state outside the window. The published observation is that agents perform perfectly for about five steps and then degrade sharply. The scratchpad and the customer record live outside the context; the context carries what this turn needs and nothing else.
  • RESOLUTION RATE VS CSATNever optimise the headline number alone. Optimise resolution and you get an agent that will not escalate. Measure reopen rate and post-escalation CSAT beside it, or the metric will be gamed by the system you just built — and you will not find out for a quarter.
  • KB FRESHNESS VS REVIEWMinutes to index, one action to roll back. Policy changes have to reach the index fast, which rules out a human review gate on every edit — so a wrong policy document propagates immediately. Version the knowledge base and make rollback a single action rather than a re-ingest.

Where the headline number hides

Intercom reports that Fin averages a 76% resolution rate across its customer base, under Intercom’s own definition, which counts procedure handoffs as resolved. One FCA-regulated customer, Carmoola, reports 60% of inbound and 90% of outbound conversations resolved end to end, under a definition that customer wrote. The industry has no standard measure: deflection is frequently counted as resolution, and abandoned chats often count too. Two vendors quoting the same figure can be measuring different things, so the first question about any of them is what it counts.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

The agent resolves 70% of tickets. Your VP wants 85%. What do you do?
Find out what the failing thirty percent actually are before you touch the system. A large slice of them are unresolvable on purpose: fraud claims, regulated disputes, customers who are not entitled to what they are asking for. Of what is left, most fail because the agent cannot do the thing rather than because it misunderstood, so the fix is new tools, not better wording. Then improve the search for the topics where it keeps missing the right article. And if more customers are coming back after a supposedly solved conversation, say so out loud — that is the target eating itself.
Segment the 30% before you change anything. Expect a large share to be structurally non-resolvable — fraud claims, regulated disputes, customers without the entitlement they are asking about — and no amount of prompt work moves those. Then, in order: add the missing tools, because most unresolved tickets fail on capability rather than comprehension; improve retrieval on the specific intents where context recall is low; and push back on the target if reopen rate is climbing, because at that point resolution and deflection are being conflated and you are being asked to game a metric. Bring the segmentation to the meeting — “85% of what?” is a legitimate answer when the definition was never written down.
How do you stop it promising a refund it cannot give?
It cannot promise, because it does not decide. The reply the customer reads is written after the refund system has answered, not before, so the agent is reporting what happened rather than predicting it. Whether a refund is allowed is settled by a separate piece of ordinary software that reads the order and the policy and never reads the chat, so nothing the customer types can talk it round. Anything above the value limit waits for a person, and a daily check lists every payment the agent started. Telling the model to be careful is not a safeguard: the same message box carries the customer trying to undo your instruction.
The model never promises — the tool layer does. The customer-facing sentence is generated after the tool returns, so the agent is describing an outcome rather than predicting one. Eligibility is decided by a deterministic policy engine reading the order, the policy version and the value threshold, and that engine never sees the conversation, so no phrasing in the chat can move it. Each tool carries an ACL, a strict output schema and an idempotency key, and anything above the threshold parks in a human approval queue. A prompt telling the model to be careful is not a control, because the channel carrying your instruction also carries the customer’s attempt to override it.
How do you evaluate this?
Score the work, not just the answer. Break each conversation into the steps it should have completed and mark them off, so a half-solved case scores as half. Check whether the agent used the right tools in the right order or called the same one three times. Check whether a right answer came from right reasoning, because a lucky one will not repeat. Then measure the business outcome: how many were solved under your written definition, how many customers came back within a week, how many needed a person, and how those people rated it afterwards. Build the test set out of real escalations, and confirm your automatic grader agrees with human graders before you believe it.
Four layers, and the business one is not optional. Task completion decomposed into sub-goals, so a partial resolution scores as partial rather than as failure. Tool-usage efficiency: redundant calls, mis-ordered calls, the same call twice. Reasoning coherence, which catches the right answer reached by wrong reasoning — the one that will not generalise to the next ticket. Then the business layer: resolution under your written definition, reopen rate, escalation rate, and CSAT after escalation. Build the golden set from real escalations rather than imagined cases, calibrate the judge against human labels to Spearman ≥0.85 before you trust a single score it produces, and sample 10% of live conversations continuously alongside 100% of escalations.

No-hire answer vs strong answer

No hire

Draws an agent with a list of tools, says “we would use LangGraph”, never bounds the loop, never prices a conversation, treats resolution rate as a self-evident metric, and has nothing for the irreversible-action problem beyond “we would prompt it carefully”.

Strong

Insists on a written definition of resolution before designing anything. Puts authority in the tool layer and says so in one sentence. Bounds the loop with a step cap, a per-task dollar cap and repetition detection, with the numbers attached. Routes ~70% of traffic to a small model and shows the $45K → $7K arithmetic unprompted. Names the reopen-rate gaming risk before the interviewer gets there.

Say this back tomorrow

About four and a half cents a conversation, against five to eight dollars for a human ticket. Cost is not what limits this design. The price of a confidently wrong answer is.
$0.045 per AI conversation  ·  $5–$8 per human ticket  ·  cost is not the constraint
  • Write down what “resolved” means before you design against it
  • Authority lives in the tool layer; a prompt is not a control surface
  • Bound the loop in numbers: 15 steps, a per-task dollar cap, two identical calls

Unlocks

  • tool-layer authority
  • bounded agent loop
  • intent routing
  • escalation payload
  • reopen rate

Design: semantic search on a 50M-product catalogue

Augment the keyword index rather than replace it — and let the 200 ms budget tell you which queries you are allowed to rerank

Say it before drawing anything: you are adding a second way to search, not replacing the first. The catalogue gets indexed twice — once by meaning, so that “something to keep coffee hot on my desk” finds a vacuum flask that uses none of those words, and once by exact words, so that a part number finds that exact part. Every search hits both stores at once with the stock and market filters applied inside each of them, the two candidate lists are merged, some searches get a second and much more accurate ranking pass, and a business layer reorders for availability, margin and seller variety before anything reaches the page.

Meaning-search on its own fails in the exact place a shop lives. A graphics card called RTX-4090 and one called RTX-4070 read as nearly the same thing to a model trained on language, and they are completely different products at completely different prices. Brand-plus-model strings, part codes and SKUs all break the same way. Exact-word search has the opposite problem and cannot answer a description. Keeping both is not fence-sitting; it is the only configuration where both kinds of query work.

The hard part is the clock. A shopper feels search latency in a way nobody feels chat latency, so you have a fifth of a second end to end, and the accurate second-pass ranker costs about a third of that on its own. At peak you would need roughly fifty of them running at once to cover every search, which does not fit. So you sort queries first: popular repeats come out of a cache, searches that are plainly a brand or a product name skip the second pass, and only the odd, wordy, long-tail searches pay for it. That routing decision is the design, and anyone who reranks everything has quietly blown the budget.

Like a shop assistant with a stockroom list and a catalogue. The list finds the exact item code a customer reads off a receipt; the catalogue finds “the thing for keeping soup warm”. She checks both, then walks the aisle herself to put four items in the customer’s hands — but she can only afford that walk for the customers who actually need it.

Scale first. 50M products against 10M searches a day is ~116 QPS average and ~500 QPS peak at p95 200 ms, with 1% daily churn giving 500K items a day to re-embed. Now size it and watch the cost argument collapse: 50M products at ~100 tokens of title, attributes and description is 5B tokens, so a full catalogue embed is ~$100 at $0.02/M and ~$650 at $0.13/M, and the daily increment is about a dollar. Embedding is not the expensive part of this system and saying so early buys you credit, because most candidates assume the opposite.

The dimension decision is the one worth arithmetic. At 256 dimensions the raw vectors are 50M×256×4B=51 GB fp32, ~13 GB at int8; at 1,536 dimensions the same catalogue is 307 GB fp32, 77 GB int8. Add the HNSW graph at M=16 (50M×16×2×4B=6.4 GB) and the 256-dim index lands at ~19 GB in RAM on one node. That is a 6× storage-and-latency decision for a modest quality difference, Matryoshka models let you truncate without retraining, and DoorDash shipped 256 in production. Replicate for QPS, not for size. Note also where the free answer stops: pgvector is production-ready to ~10M vectors a node and reaches ~50M with pgvectorscale at p95 under 50 ms, which puts this catalogue exactly on the boundary.

Walk the request path in order. Query normalisation, spell-correction and intent detection ~15 ms → cache lookup → parallel dense ANN top-100 and BM25 top-100 with stock, market and price applied as pre-filters inside both, ~30 ms → tiered fusion ~5 ms, all-term matches boosted heavily and the vector side used as fallback → conditional cross-encoder rerank ~60 ms, tail queries only → business layer for availability, margin, promotions and seller diversity ~30 ms → hydration and serialisation ~40 ms, leaving ~20 ms of headroom. The offline path: catalogue CDC → normaliser → an LLM-written product description so that sloppy merchant copy becomes comparable text before embedding → embedding service → two sinks, ANN and inverted index → alias-based atomic swap. Every query, result set and click is logged, because that log is both your fine-tuning data and your only evidence in the conversion argument later.

Failure modes, named before you are asked. Semantic drift on identifiers: a query for A1502 returns similar laptops instead of the part, so boost exact matches hard and monitor an identifier-query slice on its own. Model migration: an upgrade invalidates 50M vectors, so dual-index, shadow, ramp and roll back — the inference bill is small here, the rebuild and rollout are the expensive part. Volatile fields in the embedding: never embed price or stock, keep them filterable and update them live. Personalisation feedback: personalised results narrow discovery and the click log then confirms the narrowing, so hold an unpersonalised control slice. Multilingual aggregation: one multilingual model underperforms per-language models on head markets, and measuring in aggregate hides one market’s regression inside the average.

Split the numbers by provenance when you quote them. The 500 QPS peak, the 51 GB and 307 GB sizings, the 6.4 GB graph and the 50 rerank slots are arithmetic you perform in the room from published unit prices and index formulas. The per-engine latencies (Qdrant p50 4 ms / p99 25 ms at 1M vectors, pgvector 18/90), the +1.3% versus +7.5% NDCG fusion result, and DoorDash’s conversion figures are reported measurements from other people’s systems. Presenting the second group as if you had measured it on your catalogue is the fastest way to have every other number you gave discounted.

Ask these before you draw anything

  • Are we replacing keyword search or augmenting it?Augmenting — and insisting on this is the first correct instinct in the whole prompt.
  • Catalogue size and churn?~50M products, ~1% change daily. That is 500K items a day to re-embed, not a full rebuild.
  • Query volume and latency SLO?~10M searches/day, p95 under 200 ms. Which is what kills unconditional reranking later.
  • What is the success metric?Null-result rate, search-to-purchase conversion, and click position. Ask now or argue about it in the follow-up.
  • Multilingual?Yes, several markets — so you measure per market, because an aggregate hides one market’s regression.
  • Do we have query logs and click data?Yes. That makes fine-tuning the embedding model viable, and it makes alpha tuning an afternoon’s work.
  • Is there an LLM in the response path?Usually not required. Ask anyway, because the answer changes the entire latency budget.
  • Who owns merchandising rules?Someone else, always. Keep them in an explicit auditable layer or you will never separate a relevance regression from a promotion.

The numbers you design against

  • CATALOGUE50M products1% changes daily, so 500K re-embeds a day
  • PEAK LOAD~500 QPS10M searches/day, ~116 QPS average
  • LATENCY SLO200 ms p95search is not chat — users feel this one
  • INDEX AT 256 DIMS~19 GBint8 plus graph; 77 GB if you keep 1,536
  • FULL RE-EMBED~$1005B tokens at $0.02/M — the rollout costs more than the inference
  • OFFLINE P@1068% → 85%DoorDash, and it bought +0.66% session conversion

The interviewer is really testing

  • Whether “augment, not replace” is the first sentence out of your mouth
  • Whether you can name the exact query that meaning-search gets wrong, with a part number in it
  • Whether the 200 ms budget survives contact with a cross-encoder, and what you drop when it does not
  • Whether “quality went up” means an offline metric or money

The trap

Saying “we embed the products, embed the search box, and return the closest matches”. That sentence has no exact-word path, no stock or price filter, no second ranking pass and no plan for the day you change the model. The related one is “now that meaning-search works we can retire the keyword index”. You cannot: part numbers, rare brand names and controlled category words are exactly what meaning-search averages away, and those queries are the ones with a customer already holding a credit card.

Saying “embed the products, embed the query, cosine similarity” — no keyword path, no filters, no reranking budget, no migration plan. The sharper version, and the one that actually gets asked: “semantic search works now, so we can drop the keyword index.” The answer is no, and the reason has to be specific rather than cultural — identifiers, rare brand names and controlled vocabulary. Then offer the measurable version: slice the query log by identifier-shaped queries and show dense-only recall on that slice before anybody decides. The third version is quieter and costs more: reranking every query, which needs 50 concurrent cross-encoder slots at peak and blows the budget on the day traffic doubles.

The arithmetic, out loud derived from published unit prices

peak load10M / 86,400 s, x ~4 peak~500 QPS
catalogue tokens50M x ~100 tokens5B tokens
full embed5B x $0.02/M~$100 once
daily churn1% x 50M = 500K items~$1/day
vectors, 256 dims50M x 256 x 4 B51 GB fp32
int8 plus HNSW at M = 1651/4 + 50M x 16 x 2 x 4 B19 GB
rerank slots at peak500 QPS x 100 ms50 concurrent

The last row is the one that changes the design. Fifty concurrent cross-encoder slots is a handful of GPUs at 50–100 ms and an impossibility at 200–400 ms on CPU — and even on GPU it spends 60 ms of a 200 ms budget on every query, including every navigational one that never needed it. Route instead: cache the head, skip the reranker on brand and product-name queries, and spend it on the tail.

The math Little’s law, at peak

concurrent rerank slots=QPS×trerank​=500×0.1s=50What it does not say: 50 slots is a handful of GPUs at 50–100 ms and flatly impossible at 200–400 ms on CPU, where the rerank alone consumes the whole 200 ms budget. The lever is not more hardware. It is fewer reranked queries.

The tradeoffs, and the sentence you say

  • HYBRID VS DENSE-ONLYHybrid, in the first minute, with a failing query in hand. “RTX-4090 and RTX-4070 are semantically near-identical and commercially unrelated.” Fusion strategy is then its own decision, not a default: plain RRF bought +1.3% NDCG over BM25 and tiered boosting bought +7.5%.
  • 256 VS 1,536 DIMENSIONS256, and say why it is cheap to try. It is a 6× index decision — 51 GB against 307 GB fp32 — for a modest quality difference, and a Matryoshka model lets you truncate without retraining, so this is a dial rather than a migration. DoorDash runs 256 in production.
  • RERANK EVERYTHING VS CONDITIONALLYConditionally, and the budget decides it, not taste. Head queries hit a cache, navigational queries skip the reranker, tail queries get it. Under load the reranker is the first rung you drop, and you keep answering rather than shedding requests.
  • OFF-THE-SHELF VS FINE-TUNEDFine-tune only when you have priced the rebuild. Click logs make it viable and it materially beats a general model on your catalogue’s vocabulary, but every fine-tune triggers a full re-embed and index swap. Tie the model cadence to the migration cost, not to research enthusiasm.
  • ALPHA TUNINGCheap, domain-specific, and worth mentioning precisely because it is cheap. ~0.3 for technical catalogue text, 0.7–0.8 for conversational queries, ~0.6 mixed — and roughly 40 labelled query-relevance pairs is enough to pick one. That is an afternoon with a large payoff.
  • RELEVANCE VS MERCHANDISINGMake the business layer explicit and auditable, never a training label. Availability, margin and seller diversity all reorder the ranker’s output. Let them leak into your labels and you will never again be able to tell a relevance regression from a promotion.

Where these numbers come from

DoorDash rebuilt search and recommendation embeddings on LLM-written content in April 2026, using Gemini-embedding-001 truncated to 256 dimensions via Matryoshka and re-embedding only changed entities. Offline precision at 10 went from 68% to 85%. Online, the same change bought a 3.65% reduction in null search rate, +0.66% core search session conversion, +7.8% on dish-specific queries and +2.4% homepage order rate. Hold those two numbers next to each other: a 17-point offline gain bought two thirds of a percent of conversion. That ratio is the normal shape of this work, and knowing it is what stops you promising a PM otherwise.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Search quality is up on your offline metric and conversion is flat. What happened?
You improved a laboratory score, not the shopping experience. Check three things in order. First, whether the newly-favoured products are out of stock or badly priced, because the merchandising layer runs after the ranker and can quietly undo it. Second, whether the gain landed on rare wordy searches that almost nobody makes, which barely touches revenue. Third, whether you improved the tenth result when shoppers only ever look at the first three. And set expectations: the best public example moved its offline score from about two thirds correct to about five sixths and got two thirds of one percent more purchases. Big laboratory gains buying small revenue gains is the normal shape of this work.
Offline relevance and purchase intent are different objectives, and you have only moved the first one. Three causes, in the order worth checking. The winning results are relevant but out of stock or badly priced, which means the business layer is undoing the ranker — slice by availability. The improvement is concentrated in tail queries that carry little revenue — slice by query-frequency band, because a large NDCG gain on the tail is a rounding error on the till. Or the metric rewards recall over ten positions while users only look at the top three — slice by position. Then calibrate the expectation: DoorDash moved offline P@10 from 68% to 85% and got +0.66% session conversion. Expecting offline gains to transfer one-for-one is the tell that somebody has never shipped one.
Semantic search works now. Can you drop the keyword index?
No, and here is the specific reason. Meaning-search is good at descriptions and bad at codes. A part number has no meaning to average over, and two graphics cards whose names differ by one digit look almost identical to it while costing hundreds of pounds apart. Those are also the searches that convert best, because the shopper already knows exactly what they want. Rather than argue, measure: pull every search that looks like a code or a model name out of the logs, run meaning-search alone over that slice, and compare what it finds against what you ship today. Then the decision has a number attached to it.
No, and the reason is specific rather than cultural. Dense retrieval fails on identifiers, rare brand names and controlled vocabulary: A1502 returns similar laptops, RTX-4090 and RTX-4070 sit next to each other in the embedding space, and part numbers have no semantics to average over. Those queries also convert at the highest rate, because the shopper already knows what they want. Then make it measurable instead of a matter of opinion: slice the query log by identifier-shaped queries, run dense-only over that slice, and report recall against the current hybrid before anyone decides. If the answer is what everybody expects, you have converted an argument into a number and kept the index.
A query comes back with zero results. What happens next?
Loosen the filters before you touch the query, and say on the page that you did. Drop the narrowest filter first, then fall back to the meaning-based search on its own, because it is nearly always the exact-word side that produced the empty page. If that still finds nothing, show the category rather than a blank screen. Then record it. A search that keeps coming back empty is telling you the catalogue is missing something people want to buy, which is a buying decision rather than a bug report. Track the share of empty searches as a headline number, because it is the first one to move when retrieval gets better.
Relax the filters, not the query, and tell the user you did. In order: drop the narrowest facet first and label it in the UI so the result set is honest; then fall back to the dense-only path, since BM25 is the usual source of a hard zero; then broaden to category-level results rather than an empty page; and finally log it as a catalogue-gap signal. That last step is the part candidates miss — a query that persistently returns nothing is a merchandising input, not just a search bug. Track null-rate as a first-class metric alongside conversion: DoorDash’s content-embedding work reported a 3.65% reduction in it, and it is the metric that moves first when retrieval improves.

No-hire answer vs strong answer

No hire

Says “embed the products, embed the query, cosine similarity” and stops. No keyword path, so identifier queries silently break. No filters, so out-of-stock items rank first. No reranking budget, so the 200 ms SLO is decoration. No plan for an embedding upgrade, so the day the model changes there is no cutover. Names a vector database brand as though that were the architecture.

Strong

Commits to hybrid in the first minute with a concrete failing query. Computes the 51 GB versus 307 GB dimension decision out loud and lands on 256. Notices that reranking every query needs 50 concurrent slots and does not fit 200 ms, then routes by intent instead. Treats null-result rate and per-market slices as first-class metrics. Prices the re-embed at ~$100 and then says the rollout is the expensive part. Separates the ranker from the merchandising layer and explains why that boundary is load-bearing.

Say this back tomorrow

Fifty million products, each stored as a list of 256 numbers. That is fifty-one gigabytes at four bytes a number, and about nineteen once you compress it and add the search graph. One machine, replicated for traffic rather than for size.
50M×256×4B=51 GB  ·  int8 + graph  ·  ≈19 GB
  • Augment the keyword index — the identifier queries are the ones that convert
  • The latency budget, not the model, decides which queries get reranked
  • Offline relevance and conversion are different objectives; expect a small transfer

Unlocks

  • hybrid retrieval
  • tiered fusion
  • Matryoshka embeddings
  • conditional reranking
  • null-result rate
